Starbase This Week (2026-10-18) | Written by @Space_Mr_Banana
There's a saying that Starbase never sleeps, and that remains true despite SpaceX taking their time preparing for the upcoming flight next month. Working on both the Launch pad and reinstalling all of Ship 40’s engines, it has not been quiet. Welcome to this week's Starbase This Week.

Production Site

After its transport from the port to the production site, finally making its trip full circle, Ship 40 had the Ship aft horizontal transport hardware attached and was subsequently lifted up rather slowly until it finally once again sat in a vertical position.

It was then moved into Megabay 2 and placed onto one of the workstands in the building. What SpaceX plans now is unknown but it's likely they will strip the heatshield in places for further inspections alongside taking close looks at the rest of the vehicle.

We still do not know what the eventual fate of Ship 40 will be, whether it is put on display or Scrapped.

Also inside of Megabay 2, Ship 42 has finally got engines again ahead of its Static fire campaign for flight 15.

If you remember a couple of weeks ago, S42 had all engines removed after flight 14, we don't know exactly why they did this but it was possibly due to engine issues experience on flight 12 and 14, or it was simply that they needed to test Ship again without engines as they did send it out to Masseys on the Cryo stand.

The newer Ship 44 also made good progress in the last week, with SpaceX rolling out its transfer tubes from Starfactory to join with the rest of the vehicle already stacked in the bay.

Moving over to Megabay 1, Booster 24 received both its final aft section (AX:2) and its landing tank. So with the lower half of the booster now complete, making up the Liquid Oxygen (LOX) tank, the next steps are to start the stacking of the Methane (CH4) tank and finally to mate the two halves, completing the full height of the vehicle.

While stacking vehicles for the upcoming flights SpaceX is also continuing work on the Gigabay, which will give a huge increase to the possible rate of production at the site as teams will be able to fully utilise their capabilities with the extra space the new building will provide.

As of this week, the first of two bridge cranes has been lifted and installed in the bay, these are capable of lifting up to 420 tonnes, each one covering one of the two aisles in Gigabay.

Starbase PEIS and Launch Site

Increasing the rate of production is all well and good, but it doesn't matter unless SpaceX is actually able to and allowed to launch however many more vehicles.

Right now, SpaceX is limited to 25 launches per year from Starbase, but a new programmatic environmental impact statement which SpaceX and the FAA are in the works on, increases that number all the way up to 456 in two phases.

The first phase increases from 25 to 100, also allowing 200 landings of Ships and Boosters combined. Phase two increases the allowed cadence from 100 to the final 456 launches per year from the site, which means a whopping 912 landings.

It was also noted that this will take several years to implement as Starship matures, but just imagine, we’ll get an average of 1.5 ish flights per day if they are able to hit that cadence.

To help improve the cadence before we get this PEIS, SpaceX has been working on upgrading pad 1 to support Starship block 3.

This week saw teams lifting the center flame bucket part into the trench alongside also beginning to install the launch mount legs, bringing the pad one step closer to being able to support a launch again. The last flight from the pad was flight 11.

Over at Pad 2 SpaceX has been in full prep mode for Flight 15, where we are expecting to see hopefully both a Booster and a Ship catch.

Teams have been preparing for this outcome by testing the chopsticks a lot.

Over multiple days we have seen the chopsticks perform various tests raising to the top of the tower and conducting movements we might see during a catch attempt.

Massey’s

Now there's been a bit of an HLS update but before we get into that…

Over at Massey’s, SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, teams were working on two vehicles primarily; Booster 23 which completed only one cryogenic proof test — where they load Liquid Nitrogen and Oxygen onto the vehicle — before rolling back to the production site, and S43.1, a Ship nosecone + headertanks test article.

Booster 23’s rollback having only done one is an anomaly as all previous boosters (apart from BN3 in 2021) have conducted at least two. It's unknown what the cause for this early end to the initial cryo testing is, but it's possible that SpaceX found some issue, or got everything they wanted.

Ship 43.1 is in a similar situation, only it is slightly more unfortunate as we have seen some visible damage in the form of buckling around the nosecone tip. It's likely that this occurred during a test on the 14th October. The one glint of potential good news is that SpaceX had a host of sensors around where it buckled which means that this is likely exactly what they expected to happen, suggesting that it was intentional — although that is unconfirmed.

With that bombshell (although thankfully not that catastrophic) This weeks Starbase this Week has come to an end.

When do you think Flight 15 will launch after SpaceX finally static fires both vehicles?

And how long until Pad 1 is complete?

Starbase This Week (2026-10-25) | Written by @KangasSpaceroo
Wow, what a week. Pad 1 construction continues full speed ahead. Flight 15’s vehicles continue to progress towards a flight No Earlier Than Nov. 8, with future vehicles not far behind. AND WE FINALLY GOT AN HLS UPDATE. Welcome to this week’s Starbase This Week.

Flight 15

Starting off the week, preparations for Flight 15 were well underway at Pad 2.

Late on the 18th, the dancefloor service structure was removed from Pad 2 following checkouts and any repairs post Flight 14. Following the removal of the dancefloor and over the course of 48 hours, a total of four deluge tests occurred at the pad, all four being full deluge tests including the top plate. Additionally, the booster quick disconnects performed a purge in preparation for a vehicle’s arrival.

On the 24th, Booster 22, the booster assigned for Flight 15, would be rolled and lifted onto Pad 2. Later on the 24th, a detonation suppression system test was performed on the pad. Then early on the 25th, Booster 22 would light all 33 Raptor 3.1s, Raptor 3.1?, more on that in a minute, and performed a roughly 15 second static fire.

Initial views and duration appear to have indicated that the static fire was a success which paves the way for Flight 15 in at least two weeks. Booster 22 may be removed from Pad 2 and be rolled back for any final inspections ahead of flight, or SpaceX may choose to leave the booster at the pad.

Its flight partner, Ship 42 is still in Megabay 2 awaiting a rollout to Masseys to perform its own static fire. Ship 42 is currently set to rollout to Masseys as early as 10:00 PM (22:00 CDT) on Oct. 25.

Speaking of Ship 42, we finally have confirmation from SpaceX on why engines were removed and swapped. On Oct. 23, SpaceX announced that an upgraded Raptor 3, potentially called Raptor 3.1 or Raptor 3B like how Merlin is called Merlin 1D now, would be debuting on Flight 15. This new engine has supposedly better reliability and higher thrust compared to the Raptor 3 which has been flown on all V3 flights to date.

We also received an update from Elon this week regarding the catch status of both Ship and Booster on Flight 15. SpaceX will attempt to catch both vehicles at Pad 2. The so-called “Holy Grail of Rocketry” is almost upon us.

Pad 1

Over at Pad 1, construction is still full speed ahead with the conversion of the old pad design which had launched Flights 1 through 11 to the new design that has been built at Pad 2 and LC-39A in Florida. This week the four legs which hold the OLM itself to the pad were installed over the course of a couple of days.

Production Site

Over at the production site, vehicle construction continues. On the booster side, Booster 24 received its entire forward section this week, beginning with the F2:4 on Oct. 20, and being followed by the HS-FX:3 on Oct. 22, and the F3:4 on Oct. 24. Assuming the FWD section is stacked on the AFT section in the next couple of days, B24’s construction will be the second fastest booster construction, only being outpaced a couple of days by B19.

Moving over to the ships, Ship 44 received its AX:4 section which completes major body assembly of the vehicle, barring AFT flap install. Ship 44 continues the trend of the previous ships with major body assembly taking around a month from when the N:3 section rolls from Starfactory to when the AX:4 section rolls out and is stacked.

Speaking of ship construction timelines, Ship 45’s N:3 section rolled to Megabay 2 on Oct. 23 beginning the major assembly of this vehicle. Over the course of the next three to four weeks we’ll see this vehicle rise.

Lastly for our ships, Ship 46’s nosecone was stacked onto the PL:3 section on Oct. 21, which completes major work inside Starfactory. We’ll likely see this vehicle roll out of Starfactory over to Megabay 2 once Ship 45 completes construction.

Masseys

Lastly at Starbase, Masseys saw some action this week.

Ship 43.1, our lovely nosecone test tank, performed another test this week. Last week as you may remember, Ship 43.1 experienced some crumpling as a result of testing. It appears as if the crumple was indeed expected as teams have since repaired the crumple and tested again.

Also at Masseys, Ship 43, conducted two cryo tests on Oct. 23, with both appearing to go smoothly. A road closure has since been scheduled for Oct. 25, where it’ll roll back to the Production Site and Ship 42 will roll out to Masseys.

HLS Update

We finally got one, an HLS update. The HLS update was announced on Oct. 18 to occur on Oct. 23, and we got a lot of information from it.

Starting off, Cabin 1 is in construction. Cabin 1 is the first build of the HLS cabin which will presumably first fly on the uncrewed HLS lander mission, tentatively set for sometime in 2027. Built at Starbase, Cabin 1 is looking pretty far along in construction. Window cutouts that confirm the latest renderings of Starship HLS have been cut and reinforced, but are still lacking windows, and what appears to be a sleeping area has been shown.

Moving off to the next critical piece of HLS hardware is the propellant transfer demo, where we received confirmation that the propellant transfer demo ship is in construction. This flight is also currently set for sometime in 2027.

Over at Florida, LC-39A is in final testing ahead of receiving its first vehicle for flight which is currently set to be Flight 16. The presumed vehicle pairing for Flight 16 will be Booster 23 and Ship 43 as they are the next in line for flight after Booster 22 and Ship 42. Reuse may play a factor in the timeline but not likely to affect the pairings soon.

Lastly, we received the concept of operations for Artemis IV whether that be with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon MK2 or Starship HLS. As we are Starship Tracking, we’ll cover the HLS concept of operations in this Starbase This Week, but we encourage you to check out NASA’s update about both concepts.

Starting off for Artemis IV, Starship will first launch the depot ship followed by multiple propellant transfers. Starship HLS will launch next and be refilled by the depot ship before moving to a higher orbit. The depot will receive one last round of propellant transfer before joining HLS in a higher orbit and transferring the final bit of fuel needed for Artemis IV.

Orion will launch aboard SLS into a high-Earth orbit where HLS will dock with it. HLS will then push the entire stack to the Moon, entering a low-Lunar orbit similar to Apollo.

At the moon, two crew members will board HLS and undock from Orion before descending to the Lunar surface. Following surface operations, HLS will lift off and dock with Orion. Crew, samples, and other science will transfer back to Orion where it will push itself back to Earth.

Well that’s all for this week’s Starbase This Week. Do you think both Booster 22 and Ship 42 will be caught on Flight 15?

Starbase This Week (2026-09-06) | Written by @Bastiaan_2
With SpaceX getting closer to Flight 14, vehicles for future flights are inching behind as well. A Final Tiered Environmental Assessment has been released for possible landing sites for the ship. That and more in Starbase this Week.

Production Site

Starting this week off at the Production Site, Booster 23’s liquid oxygen tank received its transfer tube in Megabay 1. This will transfer the liquid methane to the engines and also houses the liquid methane landing tank as well.

Over at Megabay 2, the possible B23 companion Ship 43 has grown this week as well. It received two AFT sections, meaning that only the transfer tubes and the last AFT section remain. So come back next week to find out if SpaceX managed to complete the stacking process for S43.

Massey’s

Speaking of ships that completed its stacking process. S42 went out for cryo testing this week. It is hard to tell how many tests S42 completed, but going off previous cryo tests it is likely that S42 completed 2 tests.

After it completed its cryo test(s), SpaceX rolled S42 back to the Production Site on Saturday. After its cryo test campaign, SpaceX is now in the process of giving S42 its engines, after which S42 will go back to Massey’s for its static fire testing campaign before it is ready for flight 15.

Staying at Massey’s for a bit longer, the testing nosecone S43.1 underwent testing as well. However, it did not get all frosty like we normally see with other test articles. S43.1 is testing the transfer tubes from the header tanks located inside at the top of the nosecone.

Hydraulic actuators push and pull through the holes inside of the nosecone, testing if they are able to handle flight loads. But you might be asking yourself, ships have performed multiple test flights already, doesn’t SpaceX already have enough data?

Before you trust a ship to fly, you try to break it on purpose.

SpaceX pulled the engines off Starship Ship 42 and rolled it back to its test site at Massey's for more cryogenic proof testing, ahead of Flight 15.

Not a failure. Not a delay story. A pressure test designed to find weak spots on the ground.

What a cryo proof test does:
• Fill the tanks with super cold liquid
• Pressurize them beyond anything they'll see in flight
• Prove the welds and domes hold when the steel is at its most brittle

Why the engines come off:
Raptors are some of the most expensive parts on the ship. Removing them protects the hardware and lets SpaceX test the tanks as a bare structure. After that, Ship 42 goes back to Mega Bay 2 to get its engines and do its own static fire.

Meanwhile:
• Booster 22 completed a full duration 33 engine static fire on October 25
• SpaceX is targeting Flight 15 for November
• The plan is to try catching both the booster and the ship

The fine print: SpaceX hasn't said why Ship 42 needed the extra tank test, and the Flight 15 date can still move.

Break it on the ground.

So it doesn't break in the sky.

Would you rather see more tests or faster launches?

Title: SpaceX Completes Three Static Fires in Three Days for Flight 15
Author: Ryan Weber
Date: October 30, 2026
Outlet: NASASpaceFlight.com
URL: https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/10/spacex-static-fires-flight-15/

In eight days, SpaceX completed all engine testing for Flight 15, some cryo-proof and catch testing for Flight 16, and lifted the top deck deluge plates onto Pad 1’s Launch Mount. This past week has been one of the busiest in Starship program history.

Flight 16

Progress toward Flight 16 has been strong this past week. Ship 43 rolled out to Massey’s on Oct. 22 and completed both cryo-proof tests on Oct. 23. The ship then rolled back to Mega Bay 2 on Oct. 26 to be swapped to a transport stand.

Once on the transport stand, the team rolled Ship 43 out to Pad 2 for ship catch testing. This entailed lifting Ship 43 to catch height, then lowering it to bring in the Ship Quick Disconnect (SQD). Once in line, SpaceX hooked up the SQD plate to the ship to test safing procedures for when they eventually catch a ship.

After all of that testing, Ship 43 was rolled back to Mega Bay 2 on Oct. 27 and placed on the back left work stand. Ship 43 will now receive its engines installed before heading back out for its static fire campaign.

Booster 23 rolled back out to Massey’s on Oct. 27, but after spending over two full days at the cryo station, the booster did no visible testing. It could’ve done an ambient pressure test, but there were no noticeable vents to show either way. Booster 23 then rolled back to Mega Bay 1 early on Oct. 30.

Ship 42 was rolled out to Massey’s during the late-night to early-morning hours of the 26th; during that night, there were multiple closures, and SpaceX rolled Ship 43 back from Massey’s, Ship 42 out to Massey’s, and Booster 22 back from the Launch Site. So, three separate vehicle rolls in about seven hours.

Once at Massey’s, Ship 42 completed a single-engine header tank static fire on Oct. 26 to simulate an in-space deorbit burn. To simulate this, SpaceX loads the ship with the required propellant; once the propellant load is finished, teams let it sit in the tanks and warm to the desired temperature before completing a static fire.

Then, on Oct. 27, Ship 42 completed a 60-second six-engine static fire, the normal duration for Block 3 ships. With this engine testing completed, Ship 42 rolled back to Mega Bay 2 and found a full house on Oct. 29 for final flight preparations and inspections.
